title: Natural, Organic, Certified: What the Words on the Jar Really Mean
metaTitle: Natural, organic and certified cosmetics: what they mean
description: Natural and organic are not the same. What a certification like NATRUE adds, and four questions to read a cosmetic label with confidence.
bodyHtml:
Pick up almost any cosmetic product and you will find words designed to tell you what it represents.

Natural. Organic. Plant-based. Clean. Botanical. Sustainable.

But what do these words actually mean?

For someone trying to choose natural or organic cosmetics, the difficult part is not necessarily finding information. It is understanding which claims have a defined meaning, which depend on the brand’s communication and which are backed by an independent certification standard.

“Natural” and “organic” are not the same thing

The first distinction is simple but important.

Natural and organic do not mean exactly the same thing.

In the European Union, there is currently no harmonised legal definition specifically defining a cosmetic product as “natural” or “organic”. Both are treated as cosmetic claims and are subject to common criteria intended to ensure that claims are truthful, verifiable and not misleading. However, there are no mandatory harmonised criteria or certification label specifically for natural and organic cosmetics. (NATRUE)

This is one reason consumers can encounter very different ways of communicating natural or organic qualities.

A product may talk about botanical ingredients, natural origin or organic ingredients without necessarily being certified according to a specific natural cosmetics standard.

So what does certification add?

A certification standard creates a defined set of requirements against which a product can be assessed.

NATRUE is a private, voluntary and international standard for natural and organic cosmetics. It establishes criteria covering areas such as permitted ingredients, their origin and processing, formulation and other product characteristics. (NATRUE)

Importantly, NATRUE does not certify products directly.

A brand seeking certification works with a NATRUE Approved Certifier. These independent certification bodies verify whether products meet the requirements of the NATRUE Standard. (NATRUE)

That independent verification is an important part of understanding what a certification label represents.

What does the NATRUE label mean?

The NATRUE Standard has two current certification levels for finished cosmetics: natural and organic. (NATRUE)

The requirements differ according to the type of product.

NATRUE uses 13 product categories and establishes specific requirements for natural and derived-natural substances according to the characteristics of each category. This is important because different cosmetic products have different formulations and cannot all be assessed using exactly the same percentages or criteria. (NATRUE)

For products certified at the organic level, NATRUE states that at least 95% of the ingredients of plant and animal origin contained in the cosmetic product must come from certified controlled organic farming or controlled wild collection. (NATRUE)

The standard also places restrictions on the types of substances and processing methods that can be used in certified products.

What can you check as a consumer?

You do not need to know the entire NATRUE Standard to make better-informed choices.

A useful starting point is to ask four questions.

1. What exactly does the product claim?

Look carefully at the wording.

“Natural” and “organic” are not interchangeable terms, and a reference to an organic ingredient does not necessarily mean that the finished cosmetic is certified as organic.

NATRUE’s own label guidance emphasises the importance of avoiding wording that could make consumers confuse a product certified as natural with one certified as organic. (NATRUE)

2. Is there a certification label?

If a product carries a certification label, find out what standard is behind it.

A label is useful when consumers can understand what it represents.

3. Can you verify the certification?

NATRUE provides a public database of products and raw materials carrying its label, allowing consumers to look up certified products. (NATRUE)

4. What does the standard actually require?

This is perhaps the most important question.

Different certification schemes can have different criteria.

The meaningful part of a certification is therefore not simply the logo. It is the standard, the requirements and the verification process behind it.

Certification is not the same as “safe”

All cosmetics sold in the EU must be safe for human health, whether they are natural, organic or conventional. This is a legal requirement under the EU Cosmetics Regulation, and every product must undergo a safety assessment before it can be placed on the market. Natural and organic cosmetics follow exactly the same safety rules as any other cosmetic.

So a certification such as NATRUE answers a different question: does the product meet the defined criteria of the NATRUE Standard for natural or organic cosmetics?

Why this matters for small beauty brands

For an independent cosmetics brand, explaining what makes a product natural or organic can be difficult.

A product page has limited space.

Consumers have limited time.

And technical formulation information is not always easy to communicate in a simple way.

Certification can provide a common reference point.

Instead of asking the consumer to interpret every claim independently, a brand can point to a defined standard and an independent verification process.

That does not replace transparent communication.

Brands still need to explain their products clearly.

But certification can provide another layer of information between the brand and the consumer.

A simpler way to read a cosmetic label

You don’t need to know every rule or every certification standard to make a good choice.

The next time you pick up a face cream, shampoo or body lotion, simply look for a certification label you recognise. It is a quick signal that the product’s natural or organic claims have been checked against a defined standard by an independent body.

From there, you can go as far as you like: read the ingredients, look up the product in the label’s database, or learn more about what the standard requires.

Recognising the label is not the end of the decision. It is a good place to start, and a simple way to move from “this product says it is natural” to an informed purchasing choice.
